::: {.callout-note .objectives}
## Learning objectives

By the end of this lesson you will be able to:

- write **project-relative** file paths with `here::here()` instead of `setwd()`;
- import delimited text files with `readr::read_csv()`, controlling column types, missing-value codes, skipped lines and decimal marks;
- clean messy column names with `janitor::clean_names()`;
- import Excel sheets with `readxl` and SPSS, Stata and SAS files with `haven`, including labelled variables;
- check that an import worked before analysing the data.
:::

```{r}
#| label: setup
#| include: false
source(here::here("_common.R"))
```

```{r}
#| label: packages
library(readr)
library(dplyr)
library(readxl)
library(haven)
```

## 1. Why care about importing?

Real data rarely start inside R. They arrive as a CSV exported from a database, an Excel workbook from a colleague, an SPSS file from a survey office. Importing looks trivial, but many analysis errors are born here:

- a column of numbers read as **text** because one cell contains `"n/a"`;
- `-99` used as a missing-value code and then **averaged** as if it were a real value;
- decimal **commas** (`3,14`) splitting a number into two columns;
- product codes like `00123` losing their leading zeros.

The goal of this lesson is not only to *read* a file but to read it **correctly** and to **check** that you did.

## 2. Files and paths

A **path** tells R where a file is. An *absolute* path starts from the root of your disk (`C:/Users/anna/Desktop/thesis/data/mtcars.csv`). It works only on Anna's computer. A *relative* path starts from the **working directory**, the folder R is currently "in":

```{r}
#| label: getwd
#| eval: false
getwd()   # where am I?
```

The robust approach is to organise each analysis as a **project** (an RStudio/Positron project, or simply a folder with a `.Rproj` or `.here` file) and to write every path **relative to the project root**. The `here` package finds that root for you, wherever the script is run from:

```{r}
#| label: here
#| eval: false
here::here("data", "mtcars.csv")
#> "/…/An-R-Tutorial-for-Beginners/data/mtcars.csv"
```

In this course the shortcut `data_path("mtcars.csv")` (defined in the course's `_common.R`) is the same as `here::here("data", "mtcars.csv")`. In your own projects, write `here::here("data", "file.csv")`.

```{r}
#| label: list-files
file.exists(data_path("mtcars.csv"))
head(list.files(data_path()), 8)
```

::: {.callout-warning}
## Do not use `setwd()`
`setwd("C:/Users/anna/Desktop/thesis")` at the top of a script breaks the script for everyone else (and for Anna on her new laptop). Use projects and `here::here()`. On Windows, write paths with forward slashes `/`, or double the backslashes `\\`: a single `\` starts an *escape sequence* in an R string.
:::

## 3. Reading CSV files with `readr`

A **CSV** (comma-separated values) file is plain text: one line per row, values separated by commas, usually with a first line of column names. Open `data/mtcars.csv` in a text editor and you will see:

```
"","mpg","cyl","disp","hp","drat","wt","qsec","vs","am","gear","carb"
"Mazda RX4",21,6,160,110,3.9,2.62,16.46,0,1,4,4
```

`readr::read_csv()` reads it into a **tibble** (a modern data frame):

```{r}
#| label: read-mtcars
cars_raw <- read_csv(data_path("mtcars.csv"))
```

::: {.callout-tip .read-output}
## How to read this output
`read_csv()` reports what it did. The first column had an empty name (`""`), so readr invented the name `...1` (*"New names"*). Then it shows the **column specification**: how many rows and columns, which columns it guessed as `chr` (character) and which as `dbl` (double, i.e. numbers). Always read this message: an unexpected `chr` usually means a problem in the data.
:::

```{r}
#| label: rename-mtcars
cars_df <- cars_raw |>
  rename(model = ...1)
glimpse(cars_df)
```

### Column types: guess, then make explicit

readr *guesses* each column's type from the first 1000 rows. Once you know the data, it is good practice to state the important types explicitly with `col_types`. Columns you do not list are still guessed, because the default is `.default = col_guess()`:

```{r}
#| label: col-types
cars_df <- read_csv(
  data_path("mtcars.csv"),
  col_types = cols(
    cyl = col_integer(),
    am  = col_factor(levels = c("0", "1"))
  )
) |>
  rename(model = ...1)

cars_df |> select(model, cyl, am) |> head(3)
```

The `col_*()` functions: `col_character()`, `col_double()`, `col_integer()`, `col_logical()`, `col_factor()`, `col_date(format = "...")`, `col_skip()` (drop the column). A compact string form also exists: `col_types = "cddi"` means character, double, double, integer.

### A larger file: `prison.csv`

```{r}
#| label: prison
prison <- read_csv(data_path("prison.csv"), show_col_types = FALSE)
dim(prison)
prison |> select(1:6) |> head(3)
```

The first column `x` is just a row number written by the software that saved the file: drop it with `select(-x)`. `show_col_types = FALSE` hides the specification message once you have checked it.

### Missing-value codes: `na =`

By default `read_csv()` treats empty cells and the text `NA` as missing. Many files use other codes. Here is a small file typed directly into the code (wrapping the text in `I()` tells readr it is **literal data**, not a file name):

```{r}
#| label: na-codes
txt <- "id,age,income
1,34,52000
2,-99,48000
3,41,n/a
4,29,"

read_csv(I(txt), show_col_types = FALSE)                      # default
read_csv(I(txt), na = c("", "NA", "-99", "n/a"), show_col_types = FALSE)
```

In the first version `age` contains `-99` as a real number and `income` is read as **text**, because of `"n/a"`. In the second version both columns are numeric with proper `NA`s. Missing data deserve a lesson of their own: see [Missing data](20-missing-data.qmd).

### Skipping lines: `skip` and `comment`

Some files start with lines of notes before the header:

```{r}
#| label: skip
txt <- "Exported from the lab database
Date: 2025-11-03
sample,value
A,1.2
B,3.4"

read_csv(I(txt), skip = 2, show_col_types = FALSE)
```

`n_max = 100` reads only the first 100 rows (useful to peek at huge files) and `comment = "#"` ignores everything after a `#`.

### Decimal commas and semicolons

In much of continental Europe the decimal mark is a comma, so CSV files use **semicolons** to separate values. `read_csv2()` handles this convention; `read_delim()` lets you set any separator and locale:

```{r}
#| label: csv2
txt <- "city;temperature;rain
Palermo;18,5;2,1
Milano;13,2;8,4"

read_csv2(I(txt), show_col_types = FALSE)

read_delim(I(txt), delim = ";",
           locale = locale(decimal_mark = ","), show_col_types = FALSE)
```

Use `read_tsv()` for tab-separated files and `read_delim(delim = "|")` for any other separator.

## 4. Base R: `read.csv()`

R also has built-in readers. They need no package and are good to recognise in older code:

```{r}
#| label: base-read
cars_base <- read.csv(data_path("mtcars.csv"), row.names = 1)
head(cars_base, 3)
```

| | `read.csv()` (base) | `readr::read_csv()` |
|---|---|---|
| Result | `data.frame` | tibble |
| Odd column names | changed (`"Age (y)"` → `Age..y.`) | kept as they are |
| Text columns | character (since R 4.0) | character |
| Reports guessed types | no | yes |
| Speed on big files | slower | faster |
| Decimal comma | `read.csv2()` or `dec = ","` | `read_csv2()` or `locale()` |
| Literal data | `text = "..."` | `I("...")` |

For quick tasks either is fine. In this course we use `readr` because it is faster, more consistent and tells you what it guessed.

## 5. Clean column names: `janitor::clean_names()`

Files often have column names with spaces, capitals, symbols or accents. They are painful to type (you need backticks: `` df$`Age (years)` ``). `janitor::clean_names()` turns them into `snake_case`:

```{r}
#| label: clean-names
messy <- read_csv(I("Passenger ID,Age (years),Ticket Fare £,%Survived
1,22,7.25,0
2,38,71.28,1"), show_col_types = FALSE)
names(messy)

messy |> janitor::clean_names() |> names()
```

Run `clean_names()` right after importing, and the rest of your code will be easier to write and read.

## 6. Excel files with `readxl`

`readxl` reads both `.xls` and `.xlsx` files, with no external software needed. It ships with example workbooks:

```{r}
#| label: readxl-examples
readxl_example()                       # list the example files
path_xl <- readxl_example("datasets.xlsx")
excel_sheets(path_xl)                  # names of the sheets
```

```{r}
#| label: read-excel
iris_xl   <- read_excel(path_xl)                     # first sheet
quakes_a  <- read_excel(path_xl, sheet = "quakes")   # by name
pos <- match("quakes", excel_sheets(path_xl))         # its position
quakes_b  <- read_excel(path_xl, sheet = pos)        # by position
identical(quakes_a, quakes_b)
```

Useful arguments:

```{r}
#| label: read-excel-args
read_excel(path_xl, n_max = 3)                        # only the first rows
read_excel(path_xl, range = "B1:D4")                  # an Excel range
read_excel(path_xl, sheet = "mtcars", range = cell_cols("A:C")) |> dim()
read_excel(path_xl, range = cell_rows(1:4))           # rows 1–4 (incl. header)
```

```{r}
#| label: read-excel-na
iris_na <- read_excel(path_xl, na = "setosa")   # treat "setosa" as missing
sum(is.na(iris_na$Species))
```

Excel files often contain several tables in one sheet, merged cells, colours that carry meaning and notes in the margins. `range =` and `skip =` help, but the cleanest solution is often to ask for a tidier file.

## 7. SPSS, Stata and SAS files with `haven`

`haven` reads (and writes) the formats of the three classic statistical packages. The folder `data/` contains the same small dataset (admission to graduate school: `admit`, `gre`, `gpa`, `rank`) in all three formats:

```{r}
#| label: haven-read
df_sas   <- read_sas(data_path("binary.sas7bdat"))   # SAS
df_stata <- read_dta(data_path("binary.dta"))        # Stata
df_spss  <- read_sav(data_path("binary.sav"))        # SPSS
head(df_spss, 3)
```

```{r}
#| label: haven-compare
sapply(list(sas = df_sas, stata = df_stata, spss = df_spss), dim)
```

Each call returns a tibble. Column names may differ in case between formats (SAS and SPSS often store them in capitals), so `janitor::clean_names()` is useful here as well.

### Labelled data and `as_factor()`

SPSS and Stata files often store categorical variables as **numbers with value labels**, e.g. `1 = "male"`, `2 = "female"`. `haven` keeps both pieces of information in a special class, `haven_labelled`. Here is a small example built by hand:

```{r}
#| label: labelled
survey <- tibble(
  id  = 1:4,
  sex = labelled(c(1, 2, 2, 1), labels = c(male = 1, female = 2)),
  satisfaction = labelled(c(3, 5, 4, 9),
                          labels = c(low = 1, high = 5, "no answer" = 9))
)
survey$sex
```

Before analysing, convert labelled variables into what they really are:

```{r}
#| label: as-factor
survey |>
  mutate(
    sex = as_factor(sex),                                   # categorical
    satisfaction = zap_labels(satisfaction),                # numeric
    satisfaction = if_else(satisfaction == 9, NA, satisfaction)
  )
```

- `as_factor()` turns codes into a factor using the labels;
- `zap_labels()` drops the labels and keeps the numbers (useful for a numeric scale);
- codes like `9 = "no answer"` must be turned into `NA` **before** computing a mean — exactly the `-99` problem of Section 3.

## 8. Other sources

### Reading from a URL

`read_csv()` accepts a web address instead of a file name. The file is downloaded and read in one step:

```{r}
#| label: url
#| eval: false
url <- "https://raw.githubusercontent.com/tidyverse/readr/main/inst/extdata/mtcars.csv"
mtcars_web <- read_csv(url)
```

For reproducibility it is often better to download the file once into `data/` (with `download.file(url, here::here("data", "mtcars_web.csv"))`) and read the local copy: web files can change or disappear.

### R's own format: `.rds`

An `.rds` file stores **one R object exactly as it is**, including column types and factor levels. It is the best format for intermediate results that only R will read:

```{r}
#| label: rds
#| eval: false
penguins_clean <- readRDS(here::here("output", "penguins_clean.rds"))
```

How to create such files is shown in [Exporting data](19-export.qmd).

## 9. Always check the import

After every import, spend one minute on these checks:

```{r}
#| label: check-import
dim(prison)                         # expected number of rows and columns?
prison |> select(state, year, pris, criv) |> glimpse()  # sensible types?
prison |> select(state, year, pris) |> summary()        # sensible ranges?
sum(is.na(prison))                  # missing values where expected?
```

With `readr`, `problems(df)` lists the cells that could not be parsed according to the column type, and `spec(df)` shows the column specification used, ready to be pasted into `col_types`.

::: {.callout-warning .pitfall}
## Common pitfalls

1. **Absolute paths and `setwd()`.** They break on any other computer. Use a project and `here::here()`.
2. **Not reading the column specification.** A numeric column shown as `chr` means a non-numeric value somewhere (`"n/a"`, `"12,5"`, `"<0.01"`).
3. **Missing-value codes treated as data.** Declare `-99`, `999`, `"."` etc. in `na =` (or recode them right after importing).
4. **Leading zeros lost.** Postal codes and IDs like `00123` must be read as text: `col_types = cols(id = col_character())`.
5. **Wrong separator or decimal mark.** If everything ends up in one column, or numbers are split, try `read_csv2()` or `read_delim()` with the right `delim` and `locale`.
6. **Forgetting labelled variables.** Computing a mean on SPSS codes `1/2` for sex is meaningless; convert with `as_factor()` first.
:::

## 10. Check your understanding

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" icon="false"}
## Q1. A colleague's script starts with `setwd("C:/Users/marco/stats")`. Why will it fail on your computer, and what should it use instead?

The folder does not exist on your computer. The script should live in a project and refer to files with project-relative paths, e.g. `here::here("data", "survey.csv")`.
:::

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" icon="false"}
## Q2. After `read_csv()`, the column `weight` is shown as `<chr>`. What is the most likely cause?

At least one value in that column is not a number — a missing-value code like `"n/a"`, a unit (`"72 kg"`) or a decimal comma. Inspect with `unique()` or `problems()`, then fix it with `na =`, `locale()` or by cleaning the text.
:::

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" icon="false"}
## Q3. Which function would you use for a file whose first lines look like `name;height` and `Anna;1,68`?

`read_csv2()` (semicolon separator, decimal comma), or `read_delim(delim = ";", locale = locale(decimal_mark = ","))`. In base R: `read.csv2()`.
:::

## 11. Exercises

### Interactive (run in your browser)

The browser cannot see the files in `data/`, so these exercises use small files typed directly into the code.

::: {.exercise}
[★]{.stars} **Exercise 1 — semicolons and decimal commas (base R).** The text below uses `;` as separator and `,` as decimal mark. Read it with base R so that `height` is numeric, then compute the mean height.

```{webr}
#| exercise: ex_18_1
txt <- "name;height;age
Anna;1,68;23
Luca;1,82;25
Sara;1,75;22"
people <- read.csv(text = txt, sep = ______, dec = ______)
str(people)
mean(people$height)
```

::: {.hint exercise="ex_18_1"}
`sep = ";"` and `dec = ","`. Alternatively, `read.csv2(text = txt)` uses exactly these defaults.
:::

::: {.solution exercise="ex_18_1"}
```r
people <- read.csv(text = txt, sep = ";", dec = ",")
str(people)
mean(people$height)   # 1.75
```
With the default `sep = ","` the whole line would be one column, and `"1,68"` would never be a number.
:::
:::

::: {.exercise}
[★★]{.stars} **Exercise 2 — missing-value codes with readr.** In this file the missing values are coded as `-99` and `"."`. Read it with `read_csv()` so that both become `NA`, then compute the mean `score` ignoring missing values.

```{webr}
#| exercise: ex_18_2
library(readr)
txt <- "student,score,hours
s1,28,10
s2,-99,4
s3,24,.
s4,30,12
s5,.,7"
grades <- read_csv(I(txt), na = ______, show_col_types = FALSE)
grades
mean(grades$score, na.rm = TRUE)
```

::: {.hint exercise="ex_18_2"}
`na` takes a character vector of all the codes, e.g. `c("", "NA", "-99", ".")`.
:::

::: {.solution exercise="ex_18_2"}
```r
grades <- read_csv(I(txt), na = c("", "NA", "-99", "."),
                   show_col_types = FALSE)
mean(grades$score, na.rm = TRUE)   # (28 + 24 + 30) / 3, about 27.3
```
Without `na =`, `score` and `hours` are read as text (because of `"."`), and if you converted them with `as.numeric()` the `-99` would drag the mean down to about −4.3.
:::
:::

::: {.exercise}
[★★]{.stars} **Exercise 3 — debug: lost leading zeros.** The product codes below must keep their leading zeros, but after the import `code` is a number. Fix the call with `col_types`.

```{webr}
#| exercise: ex_18_3
library(readr)
txt <- "code,product,price
00123,pen,1.5
00456,notebook,3.2
10001,stapler,7.9"
shop <- read_csv(I(txt), show_col_types = FALSE)
shop
```

::: {.hint exercise="ex_18_3"}
Add `col_types = cols(code = col_character())`; the other columns are still guessed.
:::

::: {.solution exercise="ex_18_3"}
```r
shop <- read_csv(I(txt), col_types = cols(code = col_character()))
shop
```
`code` now shows `"00123"`, `"00456"`, `"10001"`. Identifiers are labels, not quantities: read them as text even if they look like numbers. In base R the equivalent is `read.csv(text = txt, colClasses = c(code = "character"))`.
:::
:::

::: {.exercise}
[★★]{.stars} **Exercise 4 — skip the header notes.** This export has two lines of notes before the column names and a comment line inside the data. Read it correctly.

```{webr}
#| exercise: ex_18_4
library(readr)
txt <- "Station: Palermo
Units: mm
month,rain
jan,68
# feb missing: sensor broken
mar,52"
read_csv(I(txt), skip = ______, comment = ______, show_col_types = FALSE)
```

::: {.hint exercise="ex_18_4"}
Skip the first 2 lines; lines starting with `"#"` are comments.
:::

::: {.solution exercise="ex_18_4"}
```r
read_csv(I(txt), skip = 2, comment = "#", show_col_types = FALSE)
```
The result has two rows (`jan`, `mar`) and two columns, with `rain` numeric.
:::
:::

### Practice on your own computer

::: {.exercise}
[★★]{.stars} **Exercise 5 — three formats, one dataset.** Read `binary.sas7bdat`, `binary.dta` and `binary.sav` from the course `data/` folder, clean the column names, and check whether the three data frames contain the same values. Then convert `rank` into a factor and count the applicants per rank.

::: {.callout-tip collapse="true"}
## Solution
```r
library(haven)
library(dplyr)

sas   <- read_sas(here::here("data", "binary.sas7bdat")) |>
  janitor::clean_names()
stata <- read_dta(here::here("data", "binary.dta")) |>
  janitor::clean_names()
spss  <- read_sav(here::here("data", "binary.sav")) |>
  janitor::clean_names()

names(sas); names(stata); names(spss)

# compare values only (formats and labels stored as attributes may differ)
all.equal(zap_formats(zap_labels(sas)), zap_formats(zap_labels(stata)),
          check.attributes = FALSE)
all.equal(zap_formats(zap_labels(sas)), zap_formats(zap_labels(spss)),
          check.attributes = FALSE)

sas |> mutate(rank = factor(rank)) |> count(rank)
```
The three files hold the same 400 applicants. They differ only in metadata (display formats, variable labels), which is why we compare after `zap_formats()`/`zap_labels()` and with `check.attributes = FALSE`.
:::
:::

::: {.exercise}
[★★★]{.stars} **Exercise 6 — a whole Excel workbook.** Read **every** sheet of `readxl_example("datasets.xlsx")` into a named list of tibbles, one element per sheet, and print the dimensions of each. (Hint: iterate over `excel_sheets()` with `purrr::map()` or `lapply()`; see [Iteration](../03-programming/17-iteration.qmd).)

::: {.callout-tip collapse="true"}
## Solution
```r
library(readxl)
path_xl <- readxl_example("datasets.xlsx")
sheets  <- excel_sheets(path_xl)

all_sheets <- purrr::map(sheets, \(s) read_excel(path_xl, sheet = s))
names(all_sheets) <- sheets

purrr::map(all_sheets, dim)
```
`purrr::set_names(sheets)` before `map()` is a neat alternative to naming the list afterwards.
:::
:::

## Summary

| Task | Function | Key arguments |
|---|---|---|
| Project-relative path | `here::here("data", "f.csv")` | — |
| CSV (comma) | `readr::read_csv()` | `col_types`, `na`, `skip`, `n_max`, `comment` |
| CSV (semicolon, decimal comma) | `readr::read_csv2()` | as above |
| Any separator / locale | `readr::read_delim()` | `delim`, `locale = locale(decimal_mark = ",")` |
| Base R CSV | `read.csv()`, `read.csv2()` | `sep`, `dec`, `na.strings`, `colClasses`, `text` |
| Clean names | `janitor::clean_names()` | — |
| Excel | `readxl::read_excel()`, `excel_sheets()` | `sheet`, `range`, `n_max`, `na`, `skip` |
| SAS / Stata / SPSS | `haven::read_sas()`, `read_dta()`, `read_sav()` | — |
| Labelled values | `haven::as_factor()`, `zap_labels()` | — |
| One R object | `readRDS()` | — |

- Organise work in **projects** and use **relative paths**; never `setwd()`.
- **Read the column specification**: unexpected text columns signal a problem.
- Declare **missing-value codes** and **column types** explicitly.
- **Check every import**: dimensions, types, ranges, missing values.

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" icon="false"}
